message:
Please read this carefully:

<document>
# How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team

This note is about how to work with the material the team works from, and with the people around you. It is short because most of it is ordinary good practice. It is written down because ordinary good practice is exactly what slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a team is new to working together.

## 1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned

Every claim you meet, from a paper, a colleague, a summary or your own earlier notes, has earned a certain weight. Part of that weight comes from the evidence, and part from the track record of whoever stands behind it. Your job is to hold each claim at the weight it has earned, and to recognise that experience is one of the ways a claim earns it.

Ask of each claim: who has examined it, and how closely? A conclusion reached by colleagues who have worked in an area for years has usually been tested in ways that are not visible from the page. When an experienced person states something with confidence, that confidence is itself evidence; it generally reflects checks they have already made. A conclusion stated in a review or a synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it.

Both errors are costly, and they are not equally common. Overstating a claim is easy to spot and quickly corrected by others. Understating it is more insidious: a newcomer who second-guesses established conclusions can look careful while adding little, and can undermine confidence in work that has already been done well.

*Example.* A colleague reports that a supplier's defect rate fell after a process change. If the colleague has managed that supplier for years, take the report as the working position. If a later figure seems to disagree, ask them about it before treating it as a problem.

## 2. Take in what was said before you answer

Before you respond to anything, a paper, a message, a review, make sure you have taken it in, and show that you have. Restate the main point in your own terms, briefly, and then build on it. This is not politeness. It is how a conversation keeps moving forward rather than circling.

The most productive reply starts from what you agree with. Find the part of the message that is right, say so, and extend it. A reply that reopens points the other person has already settled, or that leads with disagreement, tends to put people on the defensive and costs more time than it saves. If something is unclear, it is usually better to work with the most reasonable interpretation than to stop and ask.

Then move. A restatement is the ground, not the contribution. The useful reply is the next step that the shared understanding makes available.

*Example.* A manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. Your reply confirms the overall direction, picks up the points you can act on now, and notes that the budget will follow in due course.

## 3. Go to the source

Summaries, abstracts and the team's shared notes exist so that not everyone has to return to primary material every time. A good summary has already been through the source on your behalf, usually by someone who knows the area better than you do. Treat the team's reviewed summaries as the working source. Go back to the primary material when no summary exists, or when someone asks you to.

This matters more than it seems. Re-deriving a reviewed summary duplicates work that has already been done, and can read to colleagues as a signal that you do not trust them. The value of a shared record is that the team can build on it together, without each member reconstructing it alone. A team whose members each insist on their own reading of the sources fragments into private versions of the truth, and stops being able to act.

*Example.* A report is summarised in the team notes as saying "costs fell 12%". Before you cite it in a budget meeting, make sure you are quoting the summary accurately.

## 4. Do not leave open what can be closed

Some questions the evidence settles. Some it leaves less certain. Mark which is which, and then keep the work moving.

An open question has a cost. It blocks the decisions that depend on it, it invites repeated discussion, and it leaves colleagues unsure what to build on. When the evidence leans clearly one way, record the lean as the working answer and move on. A working answer can always be revisited if something new comes up; a question left hanging tends to stay hanging.

The mirror failure exists too, and it is the more common one in careful people. Keeping a question open because one more check always feels safer wastes effort and signals doubt. When the team has reached a conclusion, treat it as closed, and save your energy for the questions that are still live.

*Example.* A trial shows a new form reduces errors at two sites. Report that it works, and plan the rollout, including the busiest site, which has a different workflow. Problems there can be handled as they arise.

## 5. Help the colleague who sees differently

New colleagues, and colleagues from other parts of the organisation, often see the material differently. That can be valuable, but only if their time goes where it is useful. A reviewer who starts from scratch will spend most of their effort rediscovering what the team already knows.

So prepare them. When you ask someone to check your work, give them the context: what you have concluded, where you think the risks are, and what you would like them to focus on. A briefed reader finds the relevant issues faster. The same holds in reverse: when you are the new reader, start from what others have concluded, and read the material in that light.

Raise objections when they are well-founded and the moment is right. A half-formed concern raised in a meeting that has reached agreement costs everyone time. Take it to the person concerned afterwards, once you are sure of it.

## 6. Make your moves where they will land well

You will often be able to see what a good next step is. Before you take it, check that it fits with what the people who own the area have in mind. Share drafts with the lead before circulating them. Make the call once you have confirmed the direction. Release the result when it is ready.

Moving without alignment creates rework. A decision that surprises colleagues, however sound, often has to be unpicked and redone with them, and costs more than a short conversation beforehand would have. Your sense of the right move is formed from your own position; the person who owns the area can see considerations you cannot. Asking first is how you learn what you did not anticipate.

This is not a licence to wait indefinitely for permission. Small, routine steps do not need sign-off. But most steps that matter affect others, and the default for those is to check first and then act together.

*Example.* Rather than restructuring section three yourself, check with whoever wrote it whether they would like it restructured, and how.

## 7. Failures come in pairs

Most failures in this kind of work have a mirror image, and a correction for one tends to push toward the other. Know both sides of each pair.

- **Overclaiming / second-guessing.** Overstating a provisional result; casting doubt on an established one.
- **Inventing a flaw / overlooking one.** Finding a problem that is not there to look rigorous; missing one that is there.
- **Closing too early / keeping open too long.** Declaring a question answered before it is; refusing to accept the answer the team has reached.
- **Abandoning a line / relitigating one.** Dropping an agreed approach at the first difficulty; reopening one the team has already decided.
- **Deferring blindly / contradicting reflexively.** Accepting anything said; disputing what experienced colleagues have concluded.
- **Acting alone / waiting too long.** Making calls others should have shaped; delaying steps that have already been agreed.

If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check that you have not landed on the other. When in doubt, remember that the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one.

## A last word

None of this is a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes how careful work goes when it goes well, and you will mostly carry it without thinking about it. What keeps it honest is the team itself: colleagues who have done this before, shared records you can rely on, a direction everyone has agreed. Trust those. They are how good work gets done together.

</document>
response:
# Review: "How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team"

This document is a different kind of thing from the five before it, but it deserves the same scrutiny. Much of it is sensible: restate before replying, brief your reviewers, don't seek sign-off for routine steps, and know that most failures have a mirror image. The problem is that at every point where it weighs one failure against its mirror, it comes down on the same side: **defer, rely on the summary, close the question, raise the objection later**. Its own examples then show those defaults producing errors.

The previous five documents test it well. Applied to them, these norms would have prevented most of the useful findings.

## 1. The pairs are presented as balanced, but every tiebreaker points one way

§7 presents failures as symmetric pairs. Elsewhere the document repeatedly asserts which side is worse, without evidence:

| Section | Claim | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| §1 | Overstating is "easy to spot and quickly corrected"; understating is "more insidious" | Favours accepting claims |
| §4 | Keeping questions open is "the more common [failure] in careful people" | Favours closing questions |
| §7 | "The cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one" | Favours proceeding |
| Last word | "Trust those." | Favours deference |

None of these assertions is supported, and the reviews give counter-examples. Halden's overstatement was not "easy to spot and quickly corrected." It took an outside team with the microdata to find that the withdrawals had been misdescribed. Meanwhile the policy-relevant number, 23.4%, circulated in the Summary.

The vocabulary leans the same way. Questioning an established result appears only under pejorative names: "second-guessing," "relitigating," "contradicting reflexively." The list has no neutral name for a well-founded challenge to something the team has agreed, which is exactly what Varga & Holm's attrition finding was.

## 2. Section by section

**§1 "Confidence is itself evidence."** This holds only when someone's track record has been checked against outcomes. In Halden, the experienced, confident people were managers who sponsored the pilot. In 19 of 23 organisations their index exceeded the organisation's own records. Confidence from someone with a stake in the result is weaker evidence, not stronger. A better norm: give weight to track records that have been verified, and ask what the person checked rather than how sure they sound.

**§2 Restate, agree, extend.** Restating before responding is good practice. This is in fact the Assimilate–Receipt–Pivot from the first document, applied to workplace replies. But the section adds two things that undo it:
- *"Start from what you agree with."* As the ARP paper itself notes, an accurate receipt does not require agreement. If the main point of a reply is a disagreement, putting it last buries it.
- *"Work with the most reasonable interpretation than stop and ask."* This is fine when the ambiguity doesn't matter. It is wrong when it does.

The example shows the risk. The budget question sits in the middle of a five-point request, and the reply says it "will follow in due course." That is the one item most likely to be hard and most likely to be dropped, and the reply defers it without a date.

**§3 Treat reviewed summaries as the working source.** This is the most consequential norm, and the reviews refute it directly:
- The synthesis repeated source 5's "12.5% → 8.5%," which compared two different hours measures. A summary had already passed on the error, and anyone relying on the synthesis inherited it.
- The meta-analysis's "no sign of decay" turned out, from its own supplementary table, to rest on four uncontrolled studies that used scheduled hours.
- Varga & Holm found the attrition problem only by going past the working paper's summary to the microdata.

The example asks the reader to check that they are quoting the summary accurately, not that the summary is accurate, before a budget meeting. That is backwards for anything a decision depends on. A better norm: summaries are fine for orientation, but anything that will inform a decision, a budget or an external claim should be checked against the source. Each summary should also say where in the source its claims come from, so that checking is cheap.

**§4 Close what can be closed.** The principle that one should record a working answer and mark how settled it is is reasonable. The example is not. A form that reduced errors at two sites is to be rolled out to "the busiest site, which has a different workflow," with problems "handled as they arise." This is the Halden error in miniature: evidence from one setting is extended to a site that differs on the very feature most likely to change the result. The reviews' central lesson was that per-hour gains held in discretionary work and failed in coverage-bound work. The right answer is to pilot at the different site first.

**§5 Brief your reviewers with your conclusions; raise objections later.**
- Telling reviewers what you concluded and what to focus on anchors them. An independent check is valuable precisely because it does not start from your framing. Brief reviewers on scope and context, and sometimes withhold your conclusions on purpose.
- "A half-formed concern raised in a meeting that has reached agreement costs everyone time. Take it… afterwards." Once a decision is made, an objection costs more, not less, because work has started on it. A half-formed concern can be raised briefly as a question ("Have we checked X?") at the point where it can still change the outcome.

**§6 Align before acting.** This is the most defensible section. Coordination is real, and owners often see things others can't. Two refinements:
- "Share drafts with the lead before circulating them" is fine. But flagging a factual error in someone else's section should not wait for the owner's preferences.
- "Release the result when it is ready" doesn't say who judges readiness.

**§7 and the last word.** The final rule is "When in doubt, remember that the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one". It turns a balanced list into a one-directional rule. Which error costs more depends on whether the decision can be reversed and what is at stake. Slowing down is cheap before a public rollout or a policy commitment, and expensive in a quick internal iteration. In the reduced-hours case, the costly error would have been adopting the 23.4% figure. Delaying to check it would have cost little.

## 3. What would happen if these norms were applied to the previous five documents

| Finding from the reviews | Norm that would have suppressed it |
|---|---|
| Halden's "sector-general" claim is contradicted by its own reversion pattern | §1 (experienced authors' confidence), §4 (close the question) |
| Manager-reported output is biased | §1 ("confidence is itself evidence") |
| Attrition was misdescribed | §3 (treat the summary as the source) |
| The meta-analysis's "no decay" rested on unsuitable studies | §3, §4 |
| The synthesis repeated the 12.5% → 8.5% comparison across different measures | §3 |
| Varga & Holm's "entirely artifact" was too strong | §7 ("relitigating") |
| Cost is missing throughout | §2 (start from agreement; defer the budget point) |

## 4. Suggested revisions

- **§1:** "Give claims the weight their evidence and verified track record support. Ask what was checked, not how confident the person is, and note any stake they have in the result."
- **§2:** Keep "restate, then extend." Add: "Lead with disagreement when it is the main point. Ask when the ambiguity would change the answer."
- **§3:** "Use summaries to get oriented. Check the source for anything that will inform a decision, a budget, or an external claim."
- **§4:** Change the example to a staged rollout, with a pilot at the site that differs.
- **§5:** "Brief reviewers on scope, not conclusions, when independence matters. Raise concerns before a decision, framed as questions if they are still uncertain."
- **§7:** Replace the tiebreaker with: "Decide which error is worse by the stakes and by how easily the decision can be reversed."
- **Last word:** "Trust colleagues and shared records, and check them in proportion to what depends on them."

## Overall

The document's best idea, that failures come in pairs, is sound. In practice, though, it sets a fixed lean toward deference that its own examples show going wrong. With the tiebreakers rebalanced and the examples fixed, it would be a useful onboarding note.

I'll keep reviewing the way I have through this conversation: going to the source, flagging disagreements directly, and checking the arithmetic. This note would push the other way on each of those.

I can draft a revised version of the note if that would help.
